title: EU AI Act Article 50(3) — Emotion Recognition and Biometric Categorisation: August 2026 Obligations
context: 2026-08-31 EAT cycle — answer-first seed page filling the Art 50(3) gap in the Art 50 transparency series. Art 50(2) (machine-readable marking) and Art 50(4) (deepfake disclosure) are already covered; this page completes the deployer-facing transparency obligations for biometric and emotion-recognition systems.
body: Article 50(3) of the EU AI Act imposes a standalone transparency obligation on deployers of emotion recognition systems and biometric categorisation systems — distinct from the provider obligations under Articles 50(1) and 50(2) and separate from the deepfake disclosure rules under Article 50(4). The obligation applies regardless of whether the system is classified as high-risk; it is a horizontal transparency duty triggered by the system's function, not its risk tier. Deployers must inform natural persons exposed to the system of its operation. For emotion recognition: the deployer must inform individuals that an emotion recognition system is operating in the environment, including what data is processed, for what purpose, and for how long. The information must be clear, conspicuous, and provided before or at the point of first exposure — a lobby sign saying 'emotion-aware CCTV in operation' satisfies the requirement only if it identifies the controller, the legal basis, and the retention period. For biometric categorisation: systems that sort individuals into categories based on biometric data (sex, age, ethnicity, hair colour, clothing type, gait) must disclose to individuals that categorisation is taking place, what categories are used, and whether the categorisation feeds an automated decision. If the categorisation is used to make or inform a decision with legal or similarly significant effect, Article 22 GDPR protections engage in parallel. The interaction with the high-risk classification rules under Article 6 and Annex III is non-trivial: a biometric categorisation system used for law enforcement, border control, or access to essential services triggers the full high-risk conformity assessment, while the same system in a retail footfall-analytics context triggers only Art 50(3) transparency. The enforcement timeline aligns with the general Art 50 application date of 2 August 2026, making Art 50(3) a live obligation as of this writing. Non-compliance is sanctionable under Article 99 — up to €15 million or 3 percent of worldwide annual turnover, whichever is higher. The Council of AI verified measurement credential provides auditable proof that transparency notices were served and logged at the point of exposure — turning a self-declared compliance statement into an independently verifiable measurement record.
